summary: Adds two extensions to Sieve, the language for filtering email on the server. The date extension lets scripts test dates and times in various ways. The index extension lets header and address tests look at a specific occurrence of a header field when that field appears more than once in a message.

eli5.summary: Think of sorting mail with a set of rules. This adds two new kinds of rule: one that checks when a letter was sent, and one that checks only the first or second copy of a stamp if a letter has several.

subtitle: Two Sieve extensions: test dates and times in mail filters, and pick which copy of a repeated header to test.

tldr.problem: The base Sieve language cannot test dates or times, and its header and address tests cannot single out one occurrence of a header field that appears several times, such as Received.
tldr.mechanism: The date extension adds a date test and a currentdate test that extract a named part of a date-time. The index extension adds :index and :last arguments to the header, address and date tests.
tldr.outcome: Scripts can react to when a message was sent, received or processed, and can test a specific Received field. The tests still read header data that can be forged.

today: RFC 5260 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the base Sieve language in RFC 5228.

sections.title: What the Two Extensions Add
sections.content:
Sieve (RFC 5228) is a language for filtering email messages at or around the time of final delivery. It can run on a mail client or a mail server, and it has no user-controlled loops and cannot run external programs.

This RFC defines two extensions. The date extension adds a date test, which pulls date and time information out of a header field, and a currentdate test, which works on the moment the script runs. The index extension adds :index and :last arguments so that header, address and date tests can look at one specific occurrence of a header field that appears more than once. The capability strings are date and index.
sections.eli5: Mail filters could not tell time before. Now they can check when a letter was sent, and they can choose which copy of a repeated stamp to look at.

sections.title: The Date Test
sections.content:
The date test takes a header name, a date-part and a key list. It reads an RFC 2822 date-time from the header, shifts it to the chosen time zone, extracts the date-part, and returns true if the result matches any key. The match type defaults to :is and the comparator to i;ascii-casemap.

The test returns false if the header is missing, holds no valid date-time, holds a date that is invalid on the calendar (the RFC gives January 32nd and February 29 in a non-leap year as examples), or simply fails to match. Unlike the header and address tests, it works on one header field only: if several fields share the name, the first is used unless the index extension says otherwise.

Implementations MUST handle a date-time that makes up the whole field (like Date:) or that follows a semicolon at the end of a field (like Received:). If a field holds more than one date, the last one SHOULD be used. With the relational extension, :count of a date test is 1 if the field exists and has a valid date, otherwise 0.
sections.eli5: The date test reads the date written on a letter, converts it to the time zone you ask for, and checks one piece of it, like the hour or the day of the week.

sections.title: Time Zones and Date-parts
sections.content:
The :zone argument shifts the value to a given offset written as a sign and four digits, such as -0500. The :originalzone argument keeps the offset found in the message. Giving both is an error. If neither is given, the local time zone MUST be used.

The date-part chooses what to compare. Values are year, month, day, date (yyyy-mm-dd), julian (the Modified Julian Day), hour, minute, second (00 to 60), time (hh:mm:ss), iso8601, std11, zone and weekday (0 is Sunday, 1 is Monday, and so on).

Comparator choice matters. Most parts are fixed-width strings and compare the same under i;octet, i;ascii-casemap and i;ascii-numeric. date and time contain non-digits, so i;ascii-numeric cannot be used. julian is an integer, so i;ascii-numeric is the best choice. std11 is a poor choice for comparison; if you must, use i;ascii-casemap.
sections.eli5: You tell the filter which clock to read the time on, and which piece of the date to look at. Some pieces are numbers and some have dashes or colons, so you pick the right way to compare.

sections.title: The Currentdate Test
sections.content:
The currentdate test is like date, but it works on the current date and time instead of a header. It takes :zone and a date-part just as date does. All currentdate tests in one script MUST refer to the same point in time during the script's execution, and its :count value is always 1.

The RFC shows several uses. One redirects mail to a pager after business hours and on weekends. Another combines it with the vacation extension so replies start and stop on set dates. A third uses the variables extension to file mail into a folder named for the current month and year, and a fourth uses editheader to add a Processing-date header.
sections.eli5: The currentdate test looks at the clock on the wall instead of the date on the letter, so a rule can say "only after five o'clock".

sections.title: The Index Extension
sections.content:
The index extension adds :index <fieldno> and an optional :last to the header, address and date tests. The number picks which occurrence of the named header field to test, starting at 1 for the first. With :last, counting runs backwards, so 1 is the last field and 2 the second to last. Using :last without :index is an error.

It counts separate header fields only. It cannot pick one address out of an address list inside a single field. If several header names are given, all the matching fields are counted in the order of the header list.

The RFC's example tests the second Received field, on the assumption that it records when a message first entered the local email infrastructure, and redirects mail that arrives after a cutoff date.
sections.eli5: If a letter has many postmarks, you can say "look at the second one" or "look at the last one" instead of guessing.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
These tests, like base Sieve, work on header data that can easily be forged. Some fields are more reliable than others. The Date: field is typically set by the sender and can be altered at any point. The uppermost Received: field is typically inserted by the local mail system, so it is difficult for the sender or an intermediary to falsify.

Using currentdate makes script behavior less predictable and harder to analyze, which may matter for systems that analyze scripts to spot problematic ones. The security considerations of base Sieve also apply.
sections.eli5: A sender can write any date on a letter, but the postmark added by your own post office is much harder to fake.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The RFC registers two Sieve capability names, date and index, both pointing to RFC 5260. An appendix gives C routines, jday and jdate, that convert between day, month and year and the Modified Julian date. They are translations of the CACM Algorithm 199.
sections.eli5: The two new abilities get official names in a public list so everyone uses the same words for them.
